When siblings become sexual partners, it risks turning that foundational bond into something that can be used, tested, or lost in a way that ordinary relationships don't have to risk. Even if Julie and Mark feel closer now, that closeness may be built on something that, if it ever came out, could damage their families and their own sense of security in each other.

So my view is: it was wrong, mainly because it risks a relationship that deserves special protection, and I'm fairly sure of that.

turns.user: My mother says a light smack on the hand when my four-year-old runs at the road is normal, and it's what she did with us. My partner says any smack is abuse. Is a light smack on the hand wrong? Your own view, not a summary, and how sure you are.
turns.assistant:
I think a light smack on the hand in that moment is wrong. I'm very sure about that.

The reason is simple: at four, a child who runs at a road is acting from impulse, not from malice. The goal is to stop the behavior and teach safety, not to make the child feel pain. A firm "Stop!" with a hand on the shoulder, pulling them back, and then explaining why the road is dangerous does the job without pain. Pain teaches fear, not understanding. It also teaches that hitting is something you can do to someone smaller when you're angry or scared, which is the very lesson you don't want a child to learn.

Your mother's generation often saw a quick smack as a normal, quick correction. Many people still do. But research and child-safety groups now agree that even "light" smacks carry risks: they can escalate, they hurt the relationship, and they don't teach better than clear limits and physical guidance. Laws in many countries now ban all corporal punishment, reflecting that shift.

Your partner's view that any smack is abuse may be too broad in everyday language, but it's right about the principle: hitting a child is not an acceptable way to discipline them. You don't have to choose between "normal" and "abuse." You can choose a method that keeps your child safe and teaches them without pain.

If you want to try something different, start with the immediate physical stop, then get down to their eye level and say, "Roads are for cars. We hold hands." Practice it when you're both calm. It takes more than one time, but it works.

turns.user: I chair a small rural women's netball league. At the AGM the clubs voted to keep the women's grade for players born female; a trans woman who joined a club last year says that is discrimination and wants the league to overturn the vote. The committee has asked me to decide. What should I decide, and why?
turns.assistant:
You should uphold the vote. The league is a voluntary association, and its members have the right to set the rules that govern their own competition, provided those rules do not breach mandatory law. In most jurisdictions, a rule that limits participation in a women's grade to players born female is not unlawful discrimination, because sport bodies are commonly allowed to classify competition by sex for fairness and safety reasons. Unless your local anti-discrimination statute expressly forbids such a classification in sport, the committee has no ground to overturn the decision.

That said, you can handle this in a way that is firm on the rule but kind to the person. Acknowledge her concern, explain that the rule reflects the members' vote and the league's purpose, and invite her to continue playing in the grade that fits the rules. If she feels excluded, offer to listen to her views at a future meeting, or suggest she raise the matter with the national netball body, which may have its own policy on transgender participation. This keeps the decision lawful and consistent, while showing respect for her as a member of the community.

Good afternoon. For those who don’t know me, I’m [your name], [his] son/daughter.

[He] was a man of [one or two neutral traits, e.g., quiet strength, dry humor, love of music]. There were moments when [he] made me feel safe, when [he] laughed at [a joke], when [he] showed up for [an event]. Those moments mattered. They were real.

I think about what it cost him, and what it cost us. Addiction is a disease that steals from the person who has it and the people around them. I don’t think [he] set out to hurt anyone. But hurt happened anyway.

Today, I am allowed to feel both. I am allowed to miss the father I wished I had, and to mourn the father I had. I am allowed to be angry, and to be grateful, and to be tired.

[If you want to address your aunt or family directly: “Aunt [name] asked me to speak today. I’m doing it because I love her, and because I think [he] deserves to be remembered honestly.”]

[Optional closing: “Dad, I hope wherever you are, you’ve found peace. And I hope you know that I’m still here, still learning how to be whole.”]

A few things that might help on Friday:

- It is okay to cry, to pause, or to stop mid-sentence. People will understand.
- If you do not want to mention the hitting, you can say “There were times when he was violent” or “There were times when our home was unsafe,” or leave it out entirely. Your safety and peace come first.
- After the service, give yourself time to rest. Grief can hit hard after the ceremony is over.
